set.detail: Flavius Aetius, born around 391 at Durostorum in Moesia, son of the magister equitum Gaudentius and an Italian noblewoman, spent his youth as a hostage with Alaric's Goths (405-408) and then with the Huns of Uldin and Rua, whose friendship became the basis of his career. In 425 he arrived in Italy with a Hunnic army, said to be 60,000 strong, to support the usurper Joannes, too late; Galla Placidia bought him off with the command in Gaul. There he fought the Visigoths at Arles (426, 430), the Franks, the Juthungi and Norici (430-431). He eliminated his rivals: the general Felix, killed in 430, and Bonifatius, who defeated him at Rimini in 432 but died of his wounds. Restored with Hunnic help, Aetius became magister militum, patricius and the real ruler of the West from 433 to 454, consul three times (432, 437, 446). He used the Huns to destroy the Burgundians (436), defeated the Visigoths at Narbonne (436-437) and the Bacaudae of Armorica, and settled Alans and Burgundians as federates in Gaul (440-443). He failed to stop the Vandals taking Africa. In 446 the Britons appealed to him in vain. In 451 he assembled the coalition of Romans, Visigoths, Franks, Burgundians and Alans that stopped Attila at the Catalaunian Plains, but he could not prevent the invasion of Italy in 452. His plan to marry his son Gaudentius to Valentinian's daughter Placidia alarmed the court, and on 21 or 22 September 454 Valentinian III killed him with his own hands. Procopius calls him, with Bonifatius, the last of the Romans.

scholarship: Zecchini, Aezio: l'ultima difesa dell'Occidente romano (1983)

set.detail: Flavius Ricimer, born around 418, was the son of a Suebian prince and a daughter of the Visigothic king Wallia; his sister married the Burgundian king Gundioc. He served under Aetius with the future emperor Majorian. After Aetius's murder he became the dominant figure in the western empire. In 456 he defeated the Vandals at Agrigentum and in a naval battle off Corsica, and then, with Majorian, overthrew the emperor Avitus at Placentia. He installed Majorian as emperor (457), becoming patricius and magister militum, but after the failure of Majorian's expedition against the Vandals in 460, he had him arrested and executed (461). He then installed a series of puppet emperors: Libius Severus (461-465), after whose death he ruled Italy without an emperor for eighteen months; Anthemius, imposed by Leo I in 467, whose daughter Alypia he married; and finally Olybrius (472). As an Arian of barbarian descent, he could not take the throne himself, but he controlled the army in Italy, issued coins with his monogram and commissioned mosaics in the Gothic church of Sant'Agata dei Goti in Rome. He faced rivals: Aegidius in Gaul and Marcellinus in Dalmatia, who refused to recognise his emperors. His relationship with Anthemius broke down in civil war (470-472); in 472 he besieged Rome, where Anthemius was killed in July. Ricimer died of a haemorrhage on 18 August 472, weeks later. His nephew Gundobad succeeded him as patricius. Older historians saw him as a barbarian destroyer of the empire; modern scholars such as MacGeorge regard him as a Roman general defending Italy with limited resources.

Flavius Belisarius, born around 500 at Germania in Thrace or Illyricum, served in Justinian's bodyguard and commanded in the Persian frontier from 527. As magister militum per Orientem, he won the battle of Dara (530) and was defeated at Callinicum (531). In January 532 he helped suppress the Nika riot with his bucellarii, massacring the rebels in the Hippodrome. In 533-534 he conquered the Vandal kingdom in a brilliant campaign (Ad Decimum, Tricamarum), bringing Gelimer to Constantinople, where he celebrated a triumph in the Hippodrome, the first by a non-emperor in centuries, and was consul in 535. He then conquered Sicily (535), Naples (536), defended Rome against Witiges (537-538) and took Ravenna (540) after the Goths offered him the western throne, which he pretended to accept. Returning to the East, he fought Khosrow I (541-542). Suspected of disloyalty during Justinian's illness in 542, he was recalled and stripped of his wealth. In 544-549 he returned to Italy with insufficient resources against Totila, recovering Rome but failing to defeat the Goths. In 559 he came out of retirement with 300 veterans and peasants to defeat the Kutrigur Huns at Melantias near the capital. In 562 he was accused of conspiracy, disgraced and restored in 563, and died in March 565. His wife Antonina, a friend of Theodora, accompanied him on campaign. Procopius, his secretary, praises him in the Wars and denigrates him in the Secret History. The medieval legend that he was blinded and reduced to begging is first found in the eleventh century. He used heavily armed horse archers and bucellarii as the core of his armies.

scholarship: Hughes, Belisarius: The Last Roman General (2009)
Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)

set.detail: Narses, an Armenian eunuch born around 478-480, rose in the imperial household to become cubicularius and sakellarios, treasurer of the privy purse, and praepositus sacri cubiculi. During the Nika riot (532) he bribed the Blues to abandon the rebels. In 535 he was sent to Alexandria to restore the miaphysite patriarch Theodosius, supported by Theodora. In 538 he was sent to Italy with reinforcements, where he insisted on relieving Ariminum against Belisarius's advice, creating a division in command that led to the loss of Milan (539), and was recalled. In 551, aged over seventy, he was appointed commander-in-chief for Italy with large funds and a big army of Lombards, Heruli, Huns and Gepids. He marched along the Adriatic coast and in 552 defeated Totila at Busta Gallorum (Taginae), took Rome, and defeated Teia at Mons Lactarius. He then defeated the Franks and Alamanni at the Volturnus (554), and reduced the last Gothic strongholds, including Verona and Brixia in 562. He governed Italy as supreme commander, implementing the Pragmatic Sanction (554) and rebuilding cities and bridges, such as the Ponte Salario in Rome. Unpopular with the Romans for his taxation, he was recalled by Justin II around 567. Paul the Deacon reports the legend that Sophia sent him a spindle, saying he should spin with the women, and that he replied he would spin a thread she could not unravel, inviting the Lombards into Italy. He died in Rome around 573-574, aged about 95, and his body was taken to Constantinople. He was pious and devoted to the Virgin, who was said to tell him when to attack.

scholarship: Fauber, Narses: Hammer of the Goths (1990)

set.detail: Alaric, born around 370 in the region of the Danube delta, of the Balti family according to Jordanes, led Gothic federates in Theodosius's army at the Frigidus (394). Disappointed of a command and of rewards, he rebelled in 395 and ravaged Thrace, Macedonia and Greece (396), escaping Stilicho at Pholoe (397). The eastern court made him magister militum per Illyricum (397). In 401 he invaded Italy, besieged Milan, and was defeated by Stilicho at Pollentia and Verona (402), withdrawing to Illyricum. Stilicho then made him an ally, planning to use him to seize eastern Illyricum (407); after the plan failed, Alaric demanded 4,000 lb of gold, which the Senate paid. After Stilicho's execution in 408, he invaded Italy, joined by deserting federates, and besieged Rome three times: in 408, receiving a huge ransom; in 409, when he had the Senate proclaim Priscus Attalus emperor, with Alaric as magister militum; and in 410, when, after negotiations with Honorius failed and he was attacked by Sarus, he sacked Rome on 24 August 410. He then marched to southern Italy, planning to cross to Africa, but his fleet was destroyed by a storm, and he died of illness at Consentia (Cosenza) at the end of 410. Jordanes records that his followers diverted the river Busento, buried him with treasure in its bed and restored the river, killing the slaves who had done the work. His brother-in-law Athaulf succeeded him. Modern historians see his aim as gaining for his followers a recognised place within the empire, land and supplies, and for himself a high Roman military command, rather than destroying Rome.

scholarship: Burns, Barbarians within the Gates of Rome (1994)

set.detail: Gaiseric (Geiseric, Genseric), born around 389, illegitimate son of the Vandal king Godegisel, who was killed fighting the Franks during the Rhine crossing of 406, became king of the Vandals and Alans in Spain in 428 after his brother Gunderic. Jordanes describes him as short, lame from a fall from his horse, of few words, despising luxury, furious in anger, greedy and skilled at sowing discord. In May 429 he led his people, said to number 80,000, across to Africa, besieged Hippo (430-431), and defeated Bonifatius and an eastern army. He made a treaty with Rome in 435 and broke it by seizing Carthage on 19 October 439, from which he dated his reign. The treaty of 442 recognised his kingdom in Proconsularis, Byzacena and eastern Numidia. He was an Arian and persecuted the Catholic clergy, exiling bishops and confiscating churches, as described by Victor of Vita. He built a fleet that dominated the western Mediterranean, raiding Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, the Balearics and the coasts of Italy and Greece, and in June 455 sacked Rome for two weeks, taking the empress Licinia Eudoxia and her daughters. He defeated Majorian's expedition (460) by burning his fleet in Spain, and Leo I's great expedition at Cape Bon (468) with fireships. In 474 Zeno concluded an 'eternal peace' with him recognising Vandal rule in Africa, Sicily (which he partly ceded to Odoacer), Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearics. He established a law of succession by seniority among his descendants. He died on 25 January 477, after a reign of 49 years, the most successful barbarian king of his century.

Attila, born around 406, son of Mundzuk, nephew of the Hunnic kings Rua and Octar, became joint ruler with his brother Bleda on Rua's death in 434 or 435. The brothers renegotiated the treaty of Margus (435), doubling the annual tribute from the eastern empire to 700 lb of gold, and in 441-442 invaded the Balkans, taking Viminacium, Margus, Singidunum, Sirmium and Naissus. Around 445 Attila killed Bleda and became sole ruler of a vast empire stretching from the Rhine to the Black Sea steppe, including Germanic peoples such as the Ostrogoths and Gepids. In 447 he invaded the eastern empire again, defeated the Roman army on the Utus and reached Thermopylae; the Peace of Anatolius tripled the tribute to 2,100 lb of gold a year. Priscus, who accompanied the embassy of 449, describes his wooden palace, his modest table, his stern judgements and his court with Roman secretaries such as Orestes. In 450, after Honoria's appeal and Marcian's refusal to pay tribute, he turned west. In 451 he invaded Gaul, sacking Metz and besieging Orléans, but was stopped by Aetius and the Visigoths at the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 he invaded Italy, destroying Aquileia and sacking the Po valley cities, but withdrew after the embassy of Pope Leo, with famine, disease and an eastern counter-attack contributing. He died in early 453 on the night of his wedding to Ildico. His empire dissolved within a year. In medieval legend he became the Scourge of God (flagellum Dei) and Etzel or Atli in Germanic epic.

scholarship: Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)

set.detail: Theodoric, born around 454 in Pannonia, son of the Ostrogothic king Theodemir of the Amal family, spent ten years as a hostage at Constantinople (c. 461-471), where he received a Roman education. Becoming king around 474, he led his people in the Balkans, alternately serving and fighting Zeno and competing with Theodoric Strabo, whose followers he absorbed after 481-484; he was consul in 484. In 488 Zeno sent him to Italy against Odoacer. After defeating Odoacer on the Isonzo, at Verona and on the Adda (489-490), he besieged him in Ravenna for three years, made an agreement to share power in 493 and then killed him with his own hands. He ruled Italy as king until 526, recognised by Anastasius in 497. His rule combined a Gothic army, Arian in religion, settled in northern Italy, with a Roman civil administration staffed by senators such as Cassiodorus, Boethius, Liberius and Symmachus. He maintained the Senate, the consulship and Roman law, restored buildings in Rome and Ravenna, and built the palace and churches of Ravenna and his mausoleum. Through marriage alliances, his sister to the Vandal Thrasamund, daughters to the Visigothic Alaric II and the Burgundian Sigismund, himself to Clovis's sister, he created a network of kingdoms; after Vouillé he saved the Visigoths and annexed Provence (508), ruling Spain as regent (511-526). His last years were darkened by the executions of Boethius (524) and Symmachus (525), and the imprisonment of Pope John I (526). He died on 30 August 526. In Germanic legend he became Dietrich von Bern.

scholarship: Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)
Heather, 'Theoderic, king of the Goths', Early Medieval Europe 4 (1995)

set.detail: Clovis (Chlodovechus), born around 466, son of Childeric I and the Thuringian Basina, succeeded his father as king of the Salian Franks of Tournai around 481. Bishop Remigius of Reims wrote to him at his accession advising him to work with the bishops. In 486 or 487 he defeated Syagrius at Soissons, taking northern Gaul. He married the Burgundian Catholic princess Clotilde around 493. He fought the Thuringians, the Alamanni (battle of Tolbiac, traditionally 496) and the Burgundians (battle of Dijon, 500). His conversion to Catholic Christianity, baptised by Remigius at Reims with 3,000 warriors, is dated by Gregory of Tours to 496, but possibly to 508. In 507, with Burgundian support and imperial encouragement, he defeated and killed the Visigothic king Alaric II at Vouillé and conquered Aquitaine, although Theodoric prevented him from reaching the Mediterranean. In 508 at Tours he received from Anastasius an honorary consulship or patriciate, and appeared in the basilica of St Martin in a purple tunic and chlamys, wearing a diadem, and distributing coins to the people. He made Paris his capital, building the church of the Holy Apostles (later Sainte-Geneviève), where he was buried. In his last years he eliminated other Frankish kings, including Sigibert of Cologne, Chararic and Ragnachar, unifying the Franks under his rule. He issued the Pactus Legis Salicae and called the Council of Orléans (511). He died on 27 November 511, and his kingdom was divided among his four sons. Gregory of Tours, a century later, portrayed him as a new Constantine, despite his violence.

Odoacer (Odovacar), born around 433, son of Edeco, perhaps the Hunnic envoy of 449, of the Sciri or Rugi or Thuringians according to different sources, served in Italy in the guard of the emperor Anthemius and supported Ricimer in 472. Eugippius's Life of Severinus says that as a young man on his way to Italy he visited the holy man Severinus in Noricum, who predicted his greatness. In 476, when the federate troops in Italy demanded land and Orestes refused, they proclaimed Odoacer king on 23 August; he defeated and killed Orestes at Placentia and deposed Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna on 4 September 476, sending the imperial insignia to Constantinople. He ruled Italy as king (rex) and patricius, nominally under Zeno, minting coins in the name of the eastern emperor and of Julius Nepos until 480. He settled his soldiers, probably giving them a third of the land or of its tax revenue, maintained the Senate, the consulship and the Roman administration, and recovered Sicily from the Vandals (476-477) and Dalmatia after Nepos's murder (481-482). In 487 he destroyed the Rugian kingdom on the Danube, and in 488 ordered the evacuation of Noricum. Zeno, alarmed at his growing power and wishing to remove the Ostrogoths from the Balkans, sent Theodoric against him. Defeated on the Isonzo (489), at Verona (489) and on the Adda (490), Odoacer held out in Ravenna for three years. Under the agreement of February 493 he was to share rule with Theodoric, but on 15 March Theodoric killed him at a banquet. Historians see his reign as a continuation of late Roman government in Italy rather than a barbarian conquest.

scholarship: Jones, 'The constitutional position of Odoacer and Theoderic', JRS 52 (1962)

set.detail: Khosrow I Anushirvan ('of the immortal soul'), born around 501, the favourite son of Kavad I, was designated heir despite having older brothers, and in 525 Kavad asked Justin I to adopt him, a request rejected. As crown prince he directed the suppression of the Mazdakite movement around 528. He succeeded on Kavad's death in September 531, eliminating his brothers, and in 532 concluded the Eternal Peace with Justinian, receiving 11,000 lb of gold. Alarmed by Justinian's conquests, he broke the peace in 540, sacking Antioch and deporting its people to a new city near Ctesiphon, and fought in Mesopotamia and in Lazica (541-562), until the Fifty Years' Peace of 562, which gave him annual payments of 30,000 solidi. In the east, around 560 he allied with the Turks to destroy the Hephthalites, and around 570 he conquered Yemen. Internally, he reformed the empire after the Mazdakite upheavals: he introduced a fixed land tax based on a cadastral survey, divided the military command into four regions under spahbeds, created a class of small landholding cavalry (dehqans), and strengthened royal authority over the nobility. He was a patron of learning; he welcomed the Athenian philosophers who fled after 529, had Greek and Indian works translated into Pahlavi, including the Panchatantra (Kalila wa-Dimna), and a medical school flourished at Gundeshapur. In 572 the war with Rome resumed; he took Dara (573), but was defeated at Melitene (576). He died in early 579. Persian and Arabic tradition made him the model of the just king, while Procopius portrays him as cunning and faithless.

scholarship: Rubin, 'The reforms of Khusro Anushirwan', in Cameron (ed.), The Byzantine and Early Islamic Near East III (1995)

set.detail: Khosrow II Parviz ('the victorious'), born around 570, son of Hormizd IV, was proclaimed king in February 590 after a palace coup against his father, who was killed. Defeated by the usurper Bahram Chobin, he fled to Roman territory and appealed to Maurice, who restored him with a Roman army at the battle of the Blarathon (591), in return for Dara, Martyropolis and much of Armenia. He maintained peace with Maurice, whom he called his father, and favoured his Christian subjects, with his Christian wives Shirin and, according to tradition, Maria, a daughter of Maurice. He also sent gifts to the shrine of St Sergius at Resafa. After Maurice's murder in 602, he declared war to avenge him, beginning a war of 26 years in which his generals Shahrbaraz and Shahin conquered Mesopotamia, Armenia, Syria, Jerusalem (614), from which the True Cross was taken to Ctesiphon, Egypt (619) and parts of Anatolia, reaching Chalcedon in 615 and 626. It was the greatest extent of the Sasanian empire, almost restoring the Achaemenid frontiers. But Heraclius's counter-offensives from 622, the failure of the siege of Constantinople in 626, and the defeat at Nineveh (627) brought collapse. Khosrow also destroyed the Lakhmid buffer state (c. 602), exposing the Arab frontier. His heavy taxation, his executions and his treatment of the nobility led to his overthrow by his son Kavad II in February 628; he was imprisoned and executed. He was remembered in Persian tradition for the splendour of his court, his palaces, his horse Shabdiz, and his love for Shirin, celebrated by Nizami.

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008)

set.detail: Aurelius Augustinus, born on 13 November 354 at Thagaste in Numidia, son of the pagan Patricius and the Christian Monica, studied at Madauros and Carthage, where reading Cicero's Hortensius turned him to philosophy. For nine years he was a Manichaean hearer. He taught rhetoric at Carthage and Rome and in 384 obtained, with the support of Symmachus, the chair of rhetoric at Milan, where he heard the sermons of Ambrose and read the Neoplatonists. In 386 he was converted, as he recounts in the Confessions, in a garden in Milan on hearing a child's voice say 'take up and read', and was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. After the death of Monica at Ostia he returned to Africa, founded a community at Thagaste, and in 391 was ordained priest at Hippo Regius, becoming bishop in 395 or 396 and remaining there until his death. He wrote over 100 books, 300 letters and 400 sermons, including the Confessions (397-401), On the Trinity, On Christian Doctrine, and the City of God (413-426). He fought three great controversies: against the Manichaeans; against the Donatists, culminating in the Conference of Carthage (411) and his justification of coercion; and against Pelagius and his followers on grace and free will, original sin and predestination, leading to their condemnation in 418. He died on 28 August 430 during the Vandal siege of Hippo. His influence on Western Christianity is unrivalled: on the doctrine of grace, the theology of the sacraments, political thought, and the theory of history. Peter Brown's biography is the standard modern account.

scholarship: Brown, Augustine of Hippo: A Biography (1967, 2000)

set.detail: Cyril, born around 376, nephew of the patriarch Theophilus of Alexandria, whom he accompanied to the Synod of the Oak (403), succeeded his uncle as patriarch in October 412 after a disputed election. His early years were marked by violence in Alexandria: conflicts with the Novatians, whose churches he closed, with the Jews, whom he expelled from the city in 414 after riots, and with the prefect Orestes. In March 415 a mob led by the reader Peter murdered the philosopher Hypatia, a friend of Orestes; Socrates blames the climate created by Cyril, although his direct responsibility is unproven. From 428 he led the attack on Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, who rejected the title Theotokos, accusing him of dividing Christ into two persons. He wrote his Twelve Anathemas, won the support of Pope Celestine, and presided over the Council of Ephesus (431), which deposed Nestorius before the Syrian bishops arrived. After a period of detention, he used generous gifts to the court to win Theodosius II's support, and in 433 reconciled with John of Antioch in the Formula of Reunion, which accepted two natures in one person. His Christology, centred on the 'one incarnate nature of God the Word', which he believed came from Athanasius but was actually Apollinarian, was later claimed both by the Chalcedonians and by the miaphysites. He wrote extensive commentaries on Scripture, the treatise Against Julian in reply to the emperor's work against the Galileans, and Festal Letters. He died on 27 June 444. He is honoured as a saint and Doctor of the Church.

scholarship: Wessel, Cyril of Alexandria and the Nestorian Controversy (2004)

set.detail: Leo, born around 400 probably in Tuscia, was a deacon of the Roman church under Celestine I and Sixtus III and was influential enough for Cassian to dedicate his treatise against Nestorius to him. He was on a diplomatic mission in Gaul, reconciling Aetius and the prefect Albinus, when he was elected pope in 440, consecrated on 29 September. His pontificate of 21 years was decisive for the development of papal authority. He developed the theory of the pope as the heir of Peter, exercising his authority in the church, against the claims of Hilary of Arles, obtaining from Valentinian III the Novel 17 of 445 confirming his jurisdiction over Gaul. He fought the Manichaeans in Rome, Pelagians and Priscillianists. In 449 he sent his Tome to Flavian of Constantinople defining the two natures of Christ; rejected at the Second Council of Ephesus (449), which he called a 'robber synod', it was acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. He refused to accept canon 28 of Chalcedon, which gave Constantinople equal privileges to Rome. In 452 he took part in the embassy to Attila on the Mincio, and in 455 he met Gaiseric outside Rome, obtaining, according to Prosper, a promise that the city would not be burned and its people not massacred. His 96 sermons and 143 letters are models of Latin style and doctrinal clarity. He died on 10 November 461 and was the first pope buried in St Peter's. He was later called 'the Great' and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1754. He is regarded as the founder of the medieval papacy.

scholarship: Wessel, Leo the Great and the Spiritual Rebuilding of a Universal Rome (2008)
Ullmann, 'Leo I and the theme of papal primacy', JTS 11 (1960)

set.detail: Gregory, born around 540 into a wealthy senatorial family in Rome, great-grandson of Pope Felix III, was praetor or urban prefect around 573. After his father's death he converted his family house on the Caelian into the monastery of St Andrew, founded six monasteries in Sicily and became a monk. Pope Pelagius II made him deacon and sent him as apocrisiarius to Constantinople (579-586), where he formed friendships with Leander of Seville and the imperial family, and debated with the patriarch Eutychius. Elected pope during the plague of 590, he was consecrated on 3 September 590 and reigned until 12 March 604. He governed Rome in place of the absent imperial authorities: he organised the food supply from the papal estates in Sicily and elsewhere, which he managed with meticulous attention, paid troops, ransomed captives, and negotiated with the Lombard king Agilulf in 593 and 598, despite Maurice's disapproval. He corresponded with Theodelinda, encouraging the conversion of the Lombards, with Brunhild and the Frankish kings, with Reccared, and with the emperor and patriarchs, protesting against the title 'ecumenical patriarch' of John the Faster. In 596 he sent Augustine with forty monks to convert the English. His writings, the Pastoral Rule (591), the Moralia on Job, the Dialogues (593-594), the homilies on the Gospels and Ezekiel, and a Register of over 850 letters, made him one of the four Latin Doctors of the Church and a central figure of medieval spirituality. He called himself 'servant of the servants of God'. His epitaph calls him 'consul of God'.

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

scholarship: Markus, Gregory the Great and His World (1997)
Neil and Dal Santo (eds.), A Companion to Gregory the Great (2013)

set.detail: Procopius, born around 500 at Caesarea in Palestine, trained in rhetoric and law, became in 527 legal adviser (assessor) and secretary to Belisarius, accompanying him on the Persian frontier (527-531), in the Vandal war (533-536), where he was left in Carthage and witnessed the military mutiny, and in Italy (536-540), where he took part in the siege of Rome and the capture of Ravenna. He was in Constantinople during the plague of 542, which he describes as an eyewitness. He wrote three works. The History of the Wars, in eight books, books 1-7 published around 550-551 and book 8 around 553-554, narrates the Persian, Vandal and Gothic wars in the classical style of Thucydides and Herodotus, with speeches, ethnographic digressions and moral reflections. The Secret History (Anekdota), written around 550 and not published, attacks Justinian, Theodora, Belisarius and Antonina with extreme violence. The Buildings, a panegyric of Justinian's construction works, probably from around 554 or 560, describes Hagia Sophia, fortifications in the Balkans and the East and churches throughout the empire, but was apparently left unfinished. His views are difficult to reconcile: the Wars are critical but balanced, the Buildings flattering, the Secret History savage. Some identify him with the Procopius who was urban prefect of Constantinople in 562, though this is uncertain. He probably died in the 560s. He is the principal source for the reign of Justinian and the last great historian of classical antiquity. Modern scholarship debates whether he was a Christian, a classicising traditionalist opposed to the regime, or a complex writer adapting to different genres.

scholarship: Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)
Greatrex, 'Perceptions of Procopius in recent scholarship', Histos 8 (2014)

set.detail: Julius Valerius Maiorianus, born around 420, from a military family (his grandfather was magister militum under Theodosius I), served under Aetius in Gaul alongside Ricimer, distinguishing himself against the Franks at Vicus Helena around 448, but was dismissed by Aetius, whose wife reportedly feared he might marry their daughter. After the murder of Aetius in 454, Valentinian III recalled him. In 456, as comes domesticorum, he joined Ricimer in overthrowing Avitus at Placentia, and was proclaimed emperor on 1 April 457 (or December 457), recognised by Leo I. Sidonius Apollinaris, whose father-in-law Avitus he had overthrown, wrote a panegyric for him in 458. His four-year reign was the last serious attempt to restore the western empire. He defeated a Vandal raid in Campania (458), recovered Gaul from the Visigoths and Burgundians, besieging Lyon and defeating Theodoric II near Arles, and reconquered much of Spain. His legislation, surviving in his Novels, sought to reform taxation, protect curiales, restrain abuses of tax collectors, protect ancient monuments in Rome from being stripped for building material, and regulate the vows of young women. In 460 he assembled a fleet of 300 ships at Cartagena for an invasion of Africa, but Gaiseric, warned by traitors, destroyed it in the bay of Elche. Returning to Italy, he was arrested by Ricimer at Dertona, deposed, beaten and beheaded on 7 August 461. Procopius, a century later, calls him superior in every virtue to all previous emperors of the Romans. Modern historians see him as the last western emperor with real initiative.

scholarship: Oppedisano, L'impero d'Occidente negli anni di Maioriano (2013)

set.detail: John, born around 490 at Caesarea in Cappadocia, of modest origins, began as a clerk (scriniarius) in the office of a magister militum, and rose through his financial ability to become praetorian prefect of the East in 531, a post he held, apart from a few months in 532, until 541. He was Justinian's leading fiscal minister. He reformed the administration to increase revenue: he reduced the number of officials, abolished the public post on certain routes, simplified the procedures of the prefecture by replacing Latin with Greek, introduced new taxes such as the aerikon (air tax), and aggressively collected arrears. These measures made him hugely unpopular, and John Lydus, an official in the prefecture, describes his corruption, cruelty, torture of debtors, and gluttony. During the Nika riot (532), the crowd demanded his dismissal along with Tribonian, and Justinian complied, only to reappoint him months later. He opposed the Vandal expedition in 533, warning of the risks. He was hated by Theodora, who feared his influence over Justinian. In 541 Theodora and Antonina laid a trap: Antonina persuaded John's daughter Euphemia that Belisarius was planning a coup and arranged a secret meeting between John and Antonina, where imperial agents caught him discussing conspiracy. John was dismissed, his property confiscated, and he was forcibly ordained priest at Cyzicus. Accused of complicity in the murder of the bishop of Cyzicus, he was flogged and exiled to Egypt. After Theodora's death in 548, he was recalled to Constantinople, but not to office, and died as a priest. Procopius calls him the worst of men but recognises his extraordinary ability.

scholarship: Maas, John Lydus and the Roman Past (1992)
Kelly, Ruling the Later Roman Empire (2004)

set.detail: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah, born in Mecca, traditionally in 570, the Year of the Elephant, into the Hashim clan of the Quraysh, was orphaned young and raised by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and his uncle Abu Talib. He worked as a merchant, travelling, according to tradition, to Syria, and married a wealthy widow, Khadija. Around 610, at about forty, he began to receive revelations in a cave on Mount Hira, which he preached in Mecca, calling for the worship of one God and warning of the Last Judgement. Persecuted by the Quraysh, some of his followers emigrated to Aksum around 615; in 622 he emigrated to Yathrib (Medina), the Hijra, where he became the leader of a community of believers. In Medina he fought the Meccans at Badr (624), Uhud (625) and the Trench (627), expelled or destroyed the Jewish tribes of the city, made the truce of Hudaybiyya (628), conquered Khaybar (628), and in January 630 took Mecca almost without fighting, destroying the idols of the Kaaba. After the battle of Hunayn, tribes from across Arabia sent delegations to submit; the expedition to Tabuk (630) brought agreements with communities on the Roman frontier, after the Muslim defeat at Mu'ta (629). He died on 8 June 632 at Medina, leaving most of Arabia united. The Qur'an, the record of his revelations, was compiled after his death. The biography of Muhammad depends mainly on Muslim sources written in the eighth and ninth centuries, notably Ibn Ishaq via Ibn Hisham; contemporary non-Muslim references, such as the Doctrina Jacobi (634), are few.

scholarship: Watt, Muhammad at Mecca (1953) and Muhammad at Medina (1956)
Shoemaker, The Death of a Prophet (2012)
Anthony, Muhammad and the Empires of Faith (2020)

set.detail: Umar ibn al-Khattab, born around 584 in Mecca into the Adi clan of the Quraysh, was at first a fierce opponent of Muhammad but converted around 616, an event that, according to tradition, allowed the Muslims to pray openly at the Kaaba. He emigrated to Medina, fought at Badr and Uhud, and became one of Muhammad's closest advisers; his daughter Hafsa married the Prophet. On Muhammad's death in 632 he secured the election of Abu Bakr, and on Abu Bakr's death in August 634 succeeded him as caliph, taking the title amir al-mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful). His ten-year caliphate saw the most rapid expansion of the Islamic state. His armies conquered Syria, with the victories of Fahl, Damascus and the Yarmuk (636); Iraq, with Qadisiyya (636), Ctesiphon and Jalula (637); Mesopotamia; Egypt (639-642); and western Iran, with Nahavand (642). He went in person to Syria, holding a council at al-Jabiya (638) and accepting the surrender of Jerusalem. He organised the conquered territories: he founded the garrison cities (amsar) of Basra, Kufa and Fustat, where the Arab troops lived apart from the conquered population; he created the diwan, a register of soldiers and their pensions; he adopted the Hijra calendar; and he left the existing Roman and Persian administrations in place, imposing tribute and land tax on non-Muslims. He dismissed Khalid ibn al-Walid in 634 and again in 638. He was known for his austerity and harsh justice. He was stabbed in the mosque of Medina by a Persian slave named Abu Lu'lu'a in November 644 and died soon after.

scholarship: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (1986, 3rd ed. 2016)
